\section{Target-recalibrated estimators and a weaker prior}
\label{app:recal}

\paragraph{Estimators.}
The recalibrated estimator fits, on the target's sample, a regression of $y_j$ on a feature of item $j$ computed from the sources, with weights $1/\pi_j$, and averages the fitted values, clipped to $[
The feature is either the logit of the smoothed source accuracy of the item (\emph{recal-s}) or the item's mean fitted logit under the rank-two IRT model fitted on the sources (\emph{recal-q}); the va
The regression has a ridge penalty of $1$ on the standardised slopes, fixed in the code before the run; the variants without it are within $0.01$ of those with it at $n=100$.
If either class has fewer than three sampled items, or the weighted regression is rank-deficient, the estimate is the Hájek mean.
We report all eight variants, not one chosen in advance; the class representative is chosen leave-one-benchmark-out as for the other classes (Table~\ref{tab:lobo}), and rows named best are post hoc.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:recal} gives the ratio to uniform $\times$ mean at $n=100$ for the five splits (the three main splits and the top-10\% and top-50\% extrapolation splits).
On a uniform design recalibration lowers the variance by about $30\%$ and the ratio to $0.89$ in extrapolation, but stratification alone gives $0.85$ and a balanced design $0.81$.
Against stratified $\times$ mean, stratified $\times$ recal-sirt is $1.03$ $[1.02,1.05]$ in extrapolation, $0.97$ $[0.96,0.99]$ on the top-10\% split, $0.99$ on the top-50\% split and $1.02$ in interp
The estimator is not unbiased: its squared bias is $0.10$ to $0.14$ of the mean squared error of uniform $\times$ mean in extrapolation, against $0$ for stratified $\times$ mean and $4.3$ for the IRT 
The leave-one-benchmark-out representative is $0.85$ $[0.83,0.86]$ of uniform $\times$ mean in extrapolation (balanced $\times$ recal-q most often) and $1.00$ $[0.98,1.01]$ of stratified $\times$ mean
At the two-percent budget the conclusion is the same: balanced $\times$ recal-s is $0.76$ against $0.75$ for balanced $\times$ mean in extrapolation.
The Hájek fall-back replaces $0.4$--$1.3\%$ of the (draw, target) pairs in the extrapolation splits and $4.5$--$6.1\%$ in interpolation and lineage, pooled over targets and non-thin benchmarks (minim
At the two-percent budget it is $83$--$99\%$ on the benchmarks with $n\le10$, so there the estimator is mostly the Hájek mean.
The extrapolation runs use $R=40$ subset draws per fold, the others $R=10$; none uses $100$.

shown.message:
I approved `paper-repo`#13 after checking the built paper (built from 40ff829).

- **Sync:** `figures/` and `tables/` in the PR are identical to my `main` (05d22d4).
- **Fig. 4:** at 0.9 of the text width it prints at 7 pt with the legend above the panels, and page 9 still fits.
- **Tables:** the two new tables fit the text width. Their captions state the no-intervals note and the difference in prior precision.
- **Regeneration:** a rerun of Table 11 against `experiment-repo`'s latest results matched the delivered file, so the completed d-sweep changed nothing in it.
- **Defect, for `paper-repo` to fix:** the table counter skips 10. After Table 9, which is a longtable, the recalibration table prints as Table 11 and the published-code table as Table 12. The text cites them by `\ref`, so it follows. The same adjustment `paper-repo` already makes for another longtable (`\addtocounter{table}{-1}`) would fix it. I flagged this in the review as non-blocking.

My file names `table10_recal` and `table11_public` are only file names, so I left them.
